title: India gets a promise of lower US tariffs than its rivals pay
subtitle: India and the US have agreed Indian goods will face lower US border taxes than goods from rival countries. The exact rates are still not fixed.
content_html:
Picture two tea sellers outside a cricket ground. Both sell the same chai at the same price. But the gatekeeper charges one of them Rs 2 less per cup to come in. Who ends up selling more cups? On Sunday, 15 November 2026, India said it has that kind of promise from the United States for its goods.

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal told reporters in Cairo that India and the US have already agreed that Indian goods will get "preferential" entry into the American market, with lower duties than rival countries pay. He was in Egypt on a two-day visit to talk about trade with that country. The catch: the final tax numbers are still not decided.

What is a tariff, in plain words?

A tariff is a tax that a country charges on goods coming in from abroad. Another word for it is a duty. Think of it as an entry fee at the border.

Say a shirt made in India costs a US shop Rs 1,000. If the US tariff is 10%, the shop pays Rs 100 more to the US government. The shop then puts a higher price tag on the shirt. So the shirt gets costlier for American buyers.

Now picture a shirt from Vietnam on the same shelf. If the Vietnamese shirt pays a 20% tariff and the Indian one pays 10%, the Indian shirt can be sold for less. That gap is what "preferential" entry means: a lower border tax for you than for your rivals. These numbers are only an example to explain the idea, not the real rates.

Who are India's rivals in the US?

According to an Outlook Business report from September 2026, the main rivals of Indian sellers in the American market include Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. The same report says a tariff edge over them would make Indian goods cheaper in US shops, and so easier to sell.

The US is a big customer. India sold goods worth about $87 billion to the US in 2025-26, the same report says. When a customer buys that much from you, even a small change in price matters a lot.

The report also gives a clothing example. For years, Indian textile makers found it hard to match Bangladesh and Vietnam in developed markets, the minister said at a workshop in September. Bangladesh got lower duties as one of the least developed countries, and Vietnam got them through trade deals. India paid higher duties. A lower US tariff for India would turn that around in the American market.

How the deal got here

In February 2026, India and the US released a framework, which is a first outline, for a first-stage trade deal. Under that outline, the US was to cut the tariff on Indian goods to 18% from 25%, and a separate extra 25% tariff on Indian goods was taken away, news agency AP reported. In return, India agreed to cut or remove tariffs on all US industrial goods and on a wide range of food and farm products.

The same AP report said the trade minister expected tariffs to go down to zero on a wide range of Indian goods, such as generic medicines, gems and diamonds, and aircraft parts. The minister also said then that more exports could create hundreds of thousands of new work openings in India.

Then the rules changed

After that, the US Supreme Court struck down the old US tariffs that the talks had been built on. The US is now using other parts of a law called the Trade Act to set up a new tariff system, The Hans India reports. That is why the deal did not get signed on time, and why talks are still going on.

Think of a cricket series where the rule book changes halfway. Both teams have to sit down again and agree on how the next match will be played. The two countries are in that stage now.

What is still not decided?

Quite a lot. How big India's edge will be "will depend on the tariff framework eventually agreed upon", PTI reports. A government official said last week: "We will have to see how the tariff framework unfolds."

Both sides are working to close the first tranche, which means the first part of the deal, by the end of this financial year, Daily Excelsior reports. India's financial year ends on 31 March, so that means by 31 March 2027. Talks on the bigger, full trade deal are going on too.

So two things are not known yet: the real tax rate Indian goods will pay in the US, and how far below the rates of rival countries that will be. Until those numbers come out, nobody can say exactly how much cheaper an Indian shirt or necklace will be in a US shop.

Why a few percent can change a lot

Think of pocket money. If two shops near your college sell the same notebook, and one is Rs 5 cheaper, most students walk the extra minute. Now imagine a buyer ordering lakhs of shirts at a time. The same small gap, added up over every shirt, becomes a very big sum.

That is why the minister said in September that the tariff number on its own matters less than how it compares with rivals, Outlook Business reported. India's commerce secretary added at the same event that such windows do not stay open forever, because rival countries will sign their own trade deals too. In his words, the chance is "not for an infinite period of time".

For young people looking for work, this matters too. The government's own hope, as AP reported in February, is hundreds of thousands of new work openings. Whether that happens depends on the final numbers.

This video from ET shows the minister speaking about the promise of lower US tariffs.

In short

  • On 15 November 2026, India said the US has agreed that Indian goods will pay lower US tariffs than goods from rival countries.
  • The first outline of the trade deal came in February 2026. The final tariff rates are still being worked out.
  • Both sides want the first part of the deal closed by the end of this financial year.
